_meta.indication: ZOKINVY is indicated in patients 12 months of age and older with a BSA of 0.39 m2 and above: to reduce the risk of mortality in Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS); and for treatment of processing-deficient Progeroid Laminopathies with either heterozygous LMNA mutation with progerin-like protein accumulation, or homozygous/compound heterozygous ZMPSTE24 mutations

pivotal_trials.design: Open-label, single-arm, no concurrent treatment control (survival compared to a separate matched natural history cohort)
pivotal_trials.population: Pediatric patients with Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) or other progeroid laminopathies
pivotal_trials.result: Pooled with ProLon2 (62 HGPS patients contributing to the survival analysis: 27 in ProLon1 and 35 in ProLon2): life span of lonafarnib-treated HGPS patients increased by an average of 3 months (95% CI -11 days, 6 months) through the first three years of follow-up and by 2.5 years (95% CI 10 months, 4.1 years) through the maximum follow-up of 11 years, compared to untreated patients

key_safety: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >=25%) include vomiting, diarrhea, infection, nausea, decreased appetite, and fatigue. In pooled trials (n=63): vomiting 90%, diarrhea 81%, infection 78%, nausea 56%, fatigue 51%, upper respiratory tract infection 51%
target_moa: Lonafarnib is a farnesyltransferase inhibitor (FTI) that inhibits farnesyltransferase to prevent farnesylation and subsequent accumulation of progerin and progerin-like proteins in the inner nuclear membrane

advisory_committee.vote: No advisory committee was held for this application; it did not raise challenging efficacy or safety issues that needed external input

summary.text: Lonafarnib received rare pediatric disease designation (October 17, 2018), breakthrough therapy designation (December 12, 2018), and orphan drug designation (originally April 18, 2011), and the NDA received priority review for its potential to reduce the risk of death for a rare, fatal disease with no approved therapies. This was a traditional (not accelerated) approval based on a survival benefit in pooled phase 2 trials versus a matched natural history cohort.
